The Arnolfini Portrait. Jan van Eyck's 1434 painting depicts a wealthy merchant and his wife in an elaborately furnished domestic interior, capturing a moment of apparent marriage vows or betrothal. The painting's exquisite detail, symbolic depth, and ambiguous narrative have made it one of the most scrutinised works of Northern Renaissance art.

The work shows Giovanni Arnolfini, a merchant from Lucca active in Bruges, and his wife in their richly appointed chamber, surrounded by symbols of fertility, fidelity, and prosperity. The single candle burning in the chandelier above them, the dog at their feet, the mirror, and scattered oranges have all been interpreted as emblems of marriage, witness-bearing, and divine blessing. Van Eyck's signature appears above the mirror as a legal notarisation: "Jan van Eyck was here"—suggesting the artist as witness to the event.

The painting measures approximately 82 by 60 centimetres and is housed in the National Gallery in London. Its meaning remains debated: was it a marriage contract, a betrothal, a fertility prayer, or simply a portrait of a couple? Its hyper-detailed realism—every texture, reflection, and symbol rendered with obsessive precision—helped establish the reputation of oil painting as the supreme medium and stands as a masterwork of van Eyck's meticulous Flemish style.
